title: River crossings
summary: Look for a wide, shallow, slow section, don’t cross water above your knees, and if in doubt, don’t cross.

list: Look for a wide, shallow, slow section, or a place where the river splits into several channels. Scout downstream first for log jams, waterfalls and other hazards that could trap you, and never cross just above rapids, falls or strainers (fallen trees and brush the current flows through).
Rivers fed by snowmelt are usually lowest in the early morning and can rise by a foot or more by late afternoon.
Unbuckle your pack’s hip belt so you can get it off fast if you fall. A pack you can’t get off can drag you under.
Face upstream. Plant a sturdy pole on the upstream side as a third leg and keep two points on the bottom at all times. Move one step at a time, crossing at an angle of about 45 degrees downstream.
Don’t cross water that comes above your knees. If in doubt, don’t cross: look elsewhere, wait, or turn back.

Very cold water, such as snowmelt, can kill. Falling in makes you gasp and panic for the first 2 to 3 minutes, and you can drown. Avoid wading or swimming in very cold water; look for another way across.

If you’re swept into fast, shallow rapids, lie on your back with your feet pointed downstream and up off the rocks, and paddle with your hands. In deep rapids, lie on your stomach, head downstream, and angle toward shore.

sources.name: National Park Service, Mount Rainier National Park, Backcountry Hikers Advised to Use Caution When Crossing Rivers (news release, 6 August 2018)
